# Linear Corridor Mesh Networking and Time Synchronization

## 1. Linear Topology Constraints

High-voltage transmission lines form elongated linear geographic corridors stretching tens or hundreds of kilometers. Standard mesh protocols designed for planar clusters fail in linear topologies due to:
* Constrained routing diversity (each tower has primarily two physical neighbors: upstream and downstream along the right-of-way).
* Cascading packet delay and duty-cycle bottlenecks across multi-hop lines.
* High radio interference and electromagnetic noise generated by corona discharge and power-frequency magnetic fields.

Sagitta addresses these physical constraints through a protocol stack optimized specifically for linear corridor topologies.

## 2. Linear Time-Slotted Channel Hopping (TSCH)

The medium access control (MAC) layer implements a slotted channel-hopping schedule synchronized across the corridor:
* Time is divided into repeating slotframes of length $N_{slots} = 101$ slots ($10\text{ ms}$ slot duration).
* Each slot is identified by a monotonically incrementing Absolute Slot Number (ASN).
* Frequency channel for slot $t$ on link $l$ hops pseudo-randomly over 16 available 2.4 GHz IEEE 802.15.4 channels ($11$ to $26$):

$$f_{channel} = F\{(ASN + ChannelOffset) \pmod{16}\}$$

The slotframe designates three distinct slot classes:
1. Upstream Corridor Conveyor Slots: Dedicated collision-free slots reserved for rapid forwarding of state vectors toward the substation gateway.
2. Downstream Command Slots: Dissemination of configuration updates and synchrophasor trigger requests.
3. Shared Contention Slots: CSMA-CA slotted Aloha for neighbor discovery, association, and event-driven fault telemetry bursts.

## 3. Corridor-Compensated Flooding Time Synchronization (FTSP)

Precision travelling wave localization and synchrophasor sampling require microsecond-grade time synchronization without continuous GPS lock (which is vulnerable to spoofing, antenna fouling, and elevated power consumption).

Sagitta implements linear Flooding Time Synchronization Protocol (FTSP):
* The substation gateway serves as the root clock master ($Node_0$, synchronized to UTC via IEEE 1588 PTP or GPS).
* Synchronization beacons are periodically flooded along the transmission line.
* Time stamping occurs at the physical radio layer at the final byte of the Start-of-Frame Delimiter (SFD) pin interrupt, eliminating MAC-layer access jitter and OS queuing latency.
* Each mote maintains an 8-point linear regression model mapping local quartz counter ticks to global corridor time, tracking oscillator drift and crystal temperature coefficient.

## 4. Linear Collection Tree Protocol (L-CTP) and Aggregation

State telemetry flows along the corridor via an adaptive Expected Transmission Count (ETX) linear routing tree:
* If a primary adjacent neighbor fails, the routing layer automatically establishes a 2-hop bridge to the subsequent tower span using boosted transmit power ($+10\text{ dBm}$).
* Intermediate nodes perform in-network spatial aggregation: adjacent span temperatures, minimum clearance, and vibration indices are packed into bit-compressed vector frames, reducing total channel utilization by over 60%.

## 5. Security Architecture (AES-128-CCM*)

All frames exchanged over the air are protected using hardware-accelerated or optimized software AES-128 in Counter with CBC-MAC (CCM*) mode:
* Provides both confidentiality and cryptographic data origin authentication.
* Monotonic 32-bit frame counters and 16-bit epoch identifiers prevent replay attacks.
* Keys are securely derived using a corridor key derivation hierarchy rooted in hardware master keys.
